pos: adj. (glad of heart, cheerful; rendering Hebrew towb and samach, Greek euthumeo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon myrige, pleasant, agreeable. In the Authorized Version the word is almost always joined to the heart — the heart is made merry, and what makes it merry tells you what a man is.
biblical_def: Merry in the Authorized Version is gladness that has reached the heart and shows in the face. Solomon states the medicine plainly: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance” (Pro 15:13). But the word is morally two-edged in Scripture, and the reader must watch which cup fills it. Wine makes Nabal's heart merry, and he dies a fool (1Sa 25:36); wine makes Amnon's heart merry, and Absalom kills him at that moment (2Sa 13:28); the rich fool tells his soul to take its ease and be merry the night God requires it (Luk 12:19). Against those stands the merriment the Father commands over a son raised from the dead: “let us eat, and be merry” (Luk 15:23). And James gives the sanctified outlet: “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jas 5:13). Mirth is not forbidden; it is directed. The question Scripture presses is never whether the heart may be merry, but whether its merriment can survive the sight of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merry as gay and noisy, jovial, cheerful, pleasant — noting the older and stronger sense of causing laughter or gladness of heart.
webster_full: MER´RY, a. Gay and noisy; jovial; exhilarated to laughter.
2. Causing laughter or mirth; as a merry jest.
3. Brisk; as a merry gale.
To make merry, to be jovial; to indulge in hilarity; to feast with mirth.
scriptures: A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.

And Abigail came to Nabal; and, behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; and Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken: wherefore she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light.
And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:
Jas 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
corruption_summary: An age that has lost the fear of God keeps the merriment and throws away the ground of it — hilarity as anesthetic, the rich fool's programme sold as self-care.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 12:19 is the exact sentence modern man lives by: take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. Our contemporaries have not improved on it; they have only industrialized it. The entertainment economy exists to keep the heart merry without ever letting it stop long enough to be examined, and the therapeutic register blesses this as “unwinding” and “treating yourself.” Scripture's verdict on that programme is not that it is excessive but that it is short — God said, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee.

The recovery is not a longer face but a different fountain. James does not answer merriment with rebuke; he answers it with psalms. The Father in Luke 15 does not merely permit the feast, He commands it. Biblical merriment is the overflow of a reconciled conscience, and it is therefore the only kind that can look at death without flinching. Nabal's merriment could not survive the morning light; the prodigal's could survive the grave.
roots_summary: Hebrew samach (H8055), to be glad, and towb lev, good of heart; Greek euphraino (G2165), to be well in mind — the word of the fatted calf and of the rich fool alike.
roots_lines: Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, be glad; the root behind Israel's feasts and behind Judges' grape-treading revels (Jdg 9:27).
Hebrew towb (H2896) — good; the idiom is literally a heart made good, for good or for ill (Est 1:10).
Greek euphraino (G2165) — to make glad, be of good cheer; used of the prodigal's feast (Luk 15:23) and of the rich fool's last night (Luk 12:19).
usage: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance” — gladness is not a private matter; it reaches the face.
“Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken” — merriment with no floor under it.
“Is any merry? let him sing psalms” — the sanctified outlet for a glad heart.

pos: adj. (blessed, well-off before God; rendering Hebrew esher, Greek makarios)
etymology: From hap, chance, fortune — the English word is built on luck. Scripture empties it of luck and fills it with covenant: happiness in the Authorized Version is not what befalls a man but Whom he belongs to.
biblical_def: Happy translates the same Hebrew and Greek words elsewhere rendered blessed, and the two must be read together. The Psalter's definition is not circumstantial but covenantal: “Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” (Psa 144:15) — the ground of it is a Person, not a portion. Proverbs makes wisdom the happy man's possession (Pro 3:13), and Job makes chastening itself a mark of happiness: “happy is the man whom God correcteth” (Job 5:17), which no theory of happiness built on comfort can absorb. James pushes it further still, counting endurance the happy estate (Jas 5:11). So the Authorized Version's happiness runs directly against the grain of the word's English root. It is not good hap. It is the settled well-being of a soul in covenant with God, and it is therefore compatible with the rod, with poverty, and with a long affliction — and incompatible with prosperity outside of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines happy as lucky, fortunate, successful, and then, more truly, as being in the enjoyment of agreeable sensations from the possession of good — adding that a man is happy only when his conscience is at peace with God.
webster_full: HAP´PY, a. Lucky; fortunate; successful.
2. Being in the enjoyment of agreeable sensations from the possession of good; enjoying pleasure from the gratification of appetites or desires.
3. Prosperous; having secure possession of good.
4. That supplies pleasure; that furnishes enjoyment; agreeable.
scriptures: Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD.
Job 5:17
Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty:
Pro 3:13
Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding.
Jas 5:11
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
corruption_summary: Happiness detached from God and redefined as a felt state, then enthroned as the end of life and the test of every doctrine — so that whatever wounds is judged false.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern West has made happiness a right, a metric, and finally a hermeneutic: a teaching is weighed by whether it makes people feel well. On that scale Job 5:17 is unintelligible — a happiness that arrives by correction, that comes with a rod in its hand. Scripture will not let happiness be a feeling-state at all. It is a verdict: the man is happy because God is his, and the verdict holds while the feelings go up and down like weather.

The pastoral damage of the inversion is severe. Where happiness is the standard, chastening reads as abandonment, endurance reads as failure, and the church learns to promise what God has not promised. Recover the Psalter's grammar — Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help (Psa 146:5) — and the sufferer is no longer disqualified from happiness by his suffering. He is told where it actually lives.
roots_summary: Hebrew esher (H835), the plural exclamation O the blessednesses of!; Greek makarios (G3107), blessed — the Beatitudes' word, rendered happy in several places by the Authorized translators.
roots_lines: Hebrew esher (H835) — happy, blessed; an exclamation rather than a description, opening the Psalter (Psa 1:1) and Pro 3:13.
Greek makarios (G3107) — blessed, happy; the word of Matthew 5, and of Rom 14:22, Happy is he that condemneth not himself.
The English root hap (chance) is precisely what the biblical words exclude — nothing in covenant happiness is left to fortune.
usage: “Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” — the definition is a Person.
“Happy is the man whom God correcteth” — the rod does not disqualify a man from blessedness.
“We count them happy which endure” — the apostolic appraisal of the long affliction.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon myrhth, from myrige, pleasant. In the Authorized Version mirth is the public, audible face of gladness — songs, tabret, and harp (Gen 31:27).
biblical_def: Mirth is gladness gone public: feasting, music, and laughter together. Scripture holds it in both hands. Nehemiah records holy mirth — the people made great mirth “because they had understood the words that were declared unto them” (Neh 8:12), which is the only unassailable ground for a festival. But Ecclesiastes runs the experiment to its end: “I will prove thee with mirth… and, behold, this also is vanity” (Ecc 2:1), and Solomon reports the discovery every reveller eventually makes — “the end of that mirth is heaviness” (Pro 14:13). Mirth cannot bear the weight of being an end. It is an excellent servant of a glad heart and a cruel master of an empty one. And in exile it becomes unbearable: Babylon demanded mirth of captives who had hung their harps upon the willows (Psa 137:3), which is the world's standing demand of the grieving church — sing us one of the songs of Zion, and be cheerful about it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mirth as social merriment, hilarity, noisy gaiety — distinguishing it from the quieter and deeper word joy.
webster_full: MIRTH, n. Social merriment; hilarity; high excitement of pleasurable feelings in company.
2. Noisy gaiety; jollity.
Mirth is the sport of the senses; joy is the delight of the soul.
scriptures: Neh 8:12
And all the people went their way to eat, and to drink, and to send portions, and to make great mirth, because they had understood the words that were declared unto them.
Ecc 2:1
I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity.
Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.
For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion.
corruption_summary: Mirth promoted from servant to saviour — an entertainment industry built on Ecclesiastes 2:1 that has never once read Ecclesiastes 2:11.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon is the first and most thorough researcher of amusement, and he published his findings: mirth proved as a way of life turns to vanity and vexation. The modern arrangement simply runs the same experiment at scale and without his honesty. Where mirth is the anesthetic of choice, Proverbs 14:13 becomes the most descriptive verse in the Bible — even in laughter the heart is sorrowful — and every honest reveller knows it by two in the morning.

Nehemiah 8 shows the alternative rather than merely forbidding the counterfeit. Great mirth is commanded there, and its cause is stated: they had understood the words. That is the order Scripture keeps. Understanding first, mirth after; the feast is a response to a text. Reverse the order and you get Psalm 137 — mirth demanded of a people with nothing to be merry about, which is not festivity but cruelty.
roots_summary: Hebrew simchah (H8057), gladness, festal joy; sason (H8342), exultation; mishteh (H4960), a drinking-feast — the three faces of biblical mirth.
roots_lines: Hebrew simchah (H8057) — gladness, mirth, festal joy; the word of Nehemiah's great mirth (Neh 8:12).
Hebrew sason (H8342) — exultation, the shout of gladness; often paired with simchah in the prophets.
Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — a feast, banquet, literally a drinking; the setting where mirth most often turns (Est 1:10).
usage: “To make great mirth, because they had understood the words” — the only durable ground of a festival.
“I will prove thee with mirth… this also is vanity” — Solomon's published experiment.
“The end of that mirth is heaviness” — the invoice always arrives.

pos: adj. (full of grief; rendering Hebrew qasheh-ruach and yagon, Greek perilupos, lupeo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon sorg, care, grief, with the intensive -ful. The Authorized Version reserves it for grief that fills a soul rather than passing over it.
biblical_def: Sorrowful describes a soul filled, not merely visited, by grief. Hannah owns the word before Eli: “I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit… but have poured out my soul before the LORD” (1Sa 1:15) — and that sentence is the whole doctrine, for it shows sorrow moving toward God rather than away. The psalmist prays from the same estate (Psa 69:29), and the LORD answers it with a promise that has no conditions attached: “I have replenished every sorrowful soul” (Jer 31:25). Above all the word belongs to Christ in Gethsemane, exceeding sorrowful, even unto death — which forever forbids the church to treat sorrow as sub-Christian. Proverbs, meanwhile, exposes the counterfeit cure: “Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful” (Pro 14:13). Merriment does not dissolve grief; it only covers it. Scripture never commands the sorrowful to cheer up. It commands them to pour out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sorrowful as full of grief on account of some loss or evil, mournful, and also as producing sorrow in others.
webster_full: SOR´ROWFUL, a. Sad; grieving for the loss of some good, or on account of some expected evil.
2. Deeply serious; depressed; dejected.
3. Producing sorrow; exciting grief; mournful; as a sorrowful accident.
4. Expressing grief; accompanied with grief; as sorrowful meat.
scriptures: And Hannah answered and said, No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD. of a
But I am poor and sorrowful: let thy salvation, O God, set me up on high.
For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.
Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.
corruption_summary: Grief medicalized into a disorder to be resolved on schedule, and a church that has forgotten how to sit with the sorrowful because it has no category for a sorrow God has not yet lifted.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic settlement treats sorrow as a malfunction with a timeline. Scripture treats it as an estate a saint may lawfully occupy, sometimes for years, and from which the truest prayers in the canon were prayed. Hannah is not rebuked for her sorrowful spirit; she is vindicated in it. The psalmist is not corrected; he is answered. A church that has absorbed the modern impatience with grief will produce Job's comforters at scale — men who cannot bear a sorrow they cannot fix.

The opposite error is equally live: sorrow cultivated as identity, nursed rather than poured out. Hannah's example forecloses both. She names the sorrow honestly and empties it before the LORD, and the text records that she went her way, and her countenance was no more sad — before any circumstance had changed. Jeremiah 31:25 stands over the whole matter as a divine undertaking: every sorrowful soul, replenished.
roots_summary: Hebrew qasheh (H7186) of spirit, hard-pressed; yagon (H3015), grief; Greek perilupos (G4036), encompassed with sorrow — the Gethsemane word.
roots_lines: Hebrew qasheh ruach (H7186, H7307) — hard or heavy of spirit; Hannah's self-description before Eli (1Sa 1:15).
Hebrew yagon (H3015) — grief, sorrow; the burden the LORD undertakes to replenish (Jer 31:25).
Greek perilupos (G4036) — surrounded by grief; used of the Lord in Gethsemane and of the rich young ruler who went away sorrowful.
usage: “I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit… I have poured out my soul before the LORD” — sorrow moving the right direction.
“I have replenished every sorrowful soul” — an unconditioned divine undertaking.
“Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful” — the counterfeit cure exposed.

pos: adj. (moved with wrath; rendering Hebrew anaph, charah, Greek orgizo)
etymology: From Old Norse angr, grief, trouble, affliction — the older sense is of something that presses a man. Scripture knows a pressing that is righteous and a pressing that is murder.
biblical_def: Angry in the Authorized Version is said of God far more often than of men, and that is the first thing to notice. “The LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD” (1Ki 11:9); He was angry with Aaron, with Moses, with Israel (2Ki 17:18). This anger is not a passion that overtakes God — He is impassible, and His wrath is the settled, holy opposition of His nature to sin, revealed in covenantal terms His people can read. Human anger, by contrast, is placed under suspicion without being forbidden outright: the man who is angry with his brother without cause is in danger of the judgment, and Paul permits it only under curfew — be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Ecclesiastes locates the danger precisely: “anger resteth in the bosom of fools” (Ecc 7:9). The sin is rarely the flash. It is the lodging.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines angry as feeling resentment, provoked, and notes the word's older application to a sore or wound — inflamed, painful, angry to the touch.
webster_full: AN´GRY, a. Feeling resentment; provoked; followed generally by with before a person.
2. Showing anger; wearing the marks of anger; caused by anger; as an angry countenance.
3. Inflamed, as a sore; red; painful.
4. In Scripture, God is said to be angry with the wicked, that is, He is displeased with their conduct and will punish them.
scriptures: And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD God of Israel, which had appeared unto him twice,
Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only.
Ecc 7:9
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
Gen 45:5
Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.
corruption_summary: Anger rebranded as authenticity and moral seriousness — a virtue signal to be cultivated — while the anger of God is quietly denied as unworthy of a loving deity.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions run in opposite directions and reinforce each other. The first makes human anger a credential: the age teaches that indignation proves sincerity, and platforms reward the permanently furious. Ecclesiastes 7:9 answers it in six words — anger resteth in the bosom of fools. Not visits. Rests. The second corruption denies divine anger altogether, treating the wrath of God as a primitive layer of the text that a mature reader outgrows. But it is the same Scripture that says God is love which says the LORD was very angry with Israel, and a god incapable of wrath at evil is not more loving; he is indifferent.

Joseph shows the sanctified alternative. He has every warrant for anger and forecloses it with doctrine, not with denial: “be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves… for God did send me before you to preserve life” (Gen 45:5). He does not pretend the brothers were innocent; he names the providence that overruled them. Anger dies in the presence of a rightly-read sovereignty, and nowhere else.
roots_summary: Hebrew anaph (H599), to breathe hard through the nose, hence to be angry; charah (H2734), to burn; Greek orgizo (G3710), to be moved with settled indignation.
roots_lines: Hebrew anaph (H599) — to snort, be angry; the vivid physical root behind the LORD's anger with Solomon (1Ki 11:9).
Hebrew charah (H2734) — to burn, be kindled; the common idiom is that anger was kindled, a fire needing fuel.
Greek orgizo (G3710) — to be provoked to settled wrath, distinct from thumos, the sudden boiling-over.
usage: “The LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned” — the cause is named, never arbitrary.
“Anger resteth in the bosom of fools” — the sin is the lodging, not the flash.
“Be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves” — Joseph kills anger with providence.

pos: n. and v. (violent, tumultuous fury; rendering Hebrew ragaz, chemah, Greek phruasso)
etymology: From Latin rabies, madness, through Old French rage. The etymology is the doctrine: Scripture presents rage as a species of madness, and always as a losing one.
biblical_def: Rage is fury that has broken its banks. Naaman turns and goes away in a rage over a river (2Ki 5:12); Asa rages against the seer who told him the truth (2Ch 16:10); Nebuchadnezzar in rage and fury commands the furnace heated (Dan 3:13). In every case the rage is directed at a word the man does not wish to hear, and in every case it accomplishes nothing it intended. The theological centre of the word is Psalm 2:1 — “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” — where the massed fury of the nations against the LORD and His Anointed is met not with counter-fury but with derision from heaven. And to Sennacherib the LORD says the decisive word: “thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my hook in thy nose” (2Ki 19:28). Rage is not merely wicked in Scripture. It is handled — bridled and led home like livestock.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rage as violent anger accompanied with furious words and gestures, and extends it to the fury of a storm, a fire, or a disease — anything raging beyond control.
webster_full: RAGE, n. Violent anger accompanied with furious words, gestures or agitation.
2. Vehemence or violent exacerbation of any thing painful; as the rage of a fever.
3. Violence of a storm; fury; as the rage of the sea.
4. Enthusiasm; rapture; extreme eagerness or passion for a thing.
scriptures: Psa 2:1
Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?
Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage.
Dan 3:13
Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Then they brought these men before the king.
Then Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house; for he was in a rage with him because of this thing. And Asa oppressed some of the people the same time.
corruption_summary: Rage industrialized — monetized by platforms, dignified as righteous protest, and excused as a symptom — while Psalm 2 files it under vanity and answers it with laughter from heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has built an economy on rage. Outrage is the reliable engine of attention, and the machinery rewards whoever supplies it, so the raging man is flattered into thinking his fury is conviction. Then the therapeutic register arrives to relabel it a symptom — something that happens to a man rather than something he does — and the last restraint falls away. Scripture grants neither dignity. Psalm 2 puts the raging of the whole earth under one word: vain. Nothing is achieved. The Anointed is set on the holy hill regardless.

Asa's rage is the pastorally instructive case, because it is a believer's. He rages at Hanani for telling him the truth, imprisons him, and oppresses the people in the same season. The pattern is exact and repeatable: rage against a true word, then punish the messenger, then spread the injury outward. The recovery is Psalm 2's own counsel — Kiss the Son. Rage ends where submission begins, and nowhere short of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragaz (H7264), to quake, be agitated; chemah (H2534), heat, burning fury; Greek phruasso (G5433), to snort like a horse — the word of Psalm 2 quoted in Acts 4.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to tremble, quake, be violently agitated; the heathen's tumult in Psa 2:1.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, poison, burning wrath; Nebuchadnezzar's rage and fury (Dan 3:13).
Greek phruasso (G5433) — to neigh or snort, of a spirited horse; Peter's congregation applies it to Herod and Pilate (Act 4:25).
usage: “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” — massed fury, filed under vanity.
“So he turned and went away in a rage” — Naaman nearly forfeits his cleansing over a river.
“He was in a rage with him because of this thing” — Asa rages at the truth and imprisons it.

pos: adj. (lifted up, haughty; rendering Hebrew ge'eh, zed, Greek huperephanos)
etymology: From Old French prud, valiant, from Late Latin prodis, useful — a word that began as praise and Scripture turns into an indictment.
biblical_def: Proud is the standing biblical name for a man who has raised himself. The verdict is blunt: “Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD” (Pro 16:5) — not displeasing merely, but an abomination, the strongest category the law has. The Psalter tracks the proud as a class: they forge lies (Psa 119:69), they hold the godly in derision (Psa 119:51), they are cursed and rebuked (Psa 119:21). Isaiah sets the day of the LORD directly against them: “the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty… and he shall be brought low” (Isa 2:12). And the New Testament states the settled divine policy in one clause quoted twice: “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jas 4:6; 1Pe 5:5). That is not God declining to help the proud. It is God actively arrayed against them — the same God whose grace runs downhill to whoever will get low enough to receive it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines proud first as having inordinate self-esteem, supercilious, arrogant — and secondarily as the good sense of just self-respect, noting that Scripture uses the word almost wholly in the bad sense.
webster_full: PROUD, a. Having inordinate self-esteem; possessing a high or unreasonable conceit of one's own excellence.
2. Arrogant; haughty; supercilious.
3. Daring; presumptuous.
4. Ostentatious; grand; as proud titles.
In Scripture, the proud are the wicked, the enemies of God, whom He beholds afar off.
scriptures: Pro 16:5
Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished.
Jas 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
Isa 2:12
For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low:
Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.
corruption_summary: The word rehabilitated wholesale — pride made a civic virtue, a season, and a parade — while the thing Scripture calls an abomination is celebrated under its own biblical name.
corruption_paragraphs: No corruption in this dictionary is more complete. The English word proud has been almost entirely reclaimed as praise: to be proud of oneself is now the sign of health, and shame — the biblical instrument of conviction — is treated as the only real sin. The culture has gone further and made pride the banner of a movement, a month, and a liturgy of its own. Scripture's sentence is unchanged and unembarrassed: an abomination to the LORD (Pro 16:5). The believer is not being quaint when he declines the vocabulary. He is refusing to call an abomination good.

The recovery is not self-loathing, which is only pride turned inward and still busy with the self. It is the exchange James names: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Those are the only two positions available, and a man is always in one of them. Isaiah 2:12 fixes the timetable — every proud and lofty thing is coming down on a day already appointed — so humility is simply the wisdom of getting low voluntarily, before the day does it involuntarily.
roots_summary: Hebrew ge'eh (H1343), lifted up, haughty; zed (H2086), insolent, presumptuous; Greek huperephanos (G5244), literally showing oneself above — the word God resists.
roots_lines: Hebrew ge'eh (H1343) — high, lofty, haughty; the proud whom the day of the LORD brings low (Isa 2:12).
Hebrew zed (H2086) — insolent, presumptuous; the proud of Psalm 119 who forge lies and deride the godly.
Greek huperephanos (G5244) — appearing above others; in Jas 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5 the object of God's active resistance.
usage: “Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD” — the strongest category the law has.
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” — two positions, and every man is in one.
“Him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer” — David's household policy.

pos: v. (to express mirth or scorn audibly; rendering Hebrew tsachaq, sachaq, la'ag, Greek gelao)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hlihhan, imitative of the sound. In Scripture the same sound serves faith, unbelief, and contempt — and the reader must always ask who is laughing at whom.
biblical_def: Laugh is one of Scripture's most morally loaded words, because it is used of God, of saints, and of scorners alike. Abraham laughs at the promise and Sarah laughs behind the tent door in unbelief (Gen 18:12), and God confronts the laugh she denied — “Nay; but thou didst laugh” (Gen 18:15). Then the same word is redeemed in the same household: “God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me” (Gen 21:6), and the child of the promise is named Isaac, he laughs. Scoffers laugh Hezekiah's messengers to scorn and Nehemiah's builders after them (Neh 2:19); Job is laughed to scorn by his neighbours (Job 12:4). And over the massed contempt of the nations, heaven laughs last — he that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh. The Lord's own beatitude promises the reversal to His people and pronounces woe on the premature laughers (Luk 6:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines laugh as to make the noise and exhibit the features which are characteristic of mirth, and secondarily as to deride or ridicule — to laugh to scorn.
webster_full: LAUGH, v.i. To make the noise and exhibit the features which are characteristic of mirth in the human species.
2. In poetry, to be gay; to appear gay, cheerful, pleasant, lively.
To laugh at, to ridicule; to treat with some degree of contempt.
To laugh to scorn, to deride; to treat with mockery, contempt and scorn.
scriptures: Gen 21:6
And Sarah said, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.
Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh.
Neh 2:19

But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?
Luk 6:25
Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep.
corruption_summary: Mockery promoted to argument — the sneer that answers a doctrine by laughing at it — while the church is shamed out of the holy laughter Scripture actually promises.
corruption_paragraphs: Laughing to scorn is the oldest substitute for refutation, and it is the dominant mode of the present age toward Scripture. Sanballat and Geshem did not answer Nehemiah's theology; they laughed and asked, what is this thing that ye do? The tactic works because it costs nothing and requires no argument, and because most men would rather be wrong than ridiculous. The believer should recognize the sneer as a confession of empty hands, and should notice that in every biblical instance the scorners are building nothing while the mocked are building a wall.

The opposite loss is subtler. A church stung by mockery often surrenders laughter altogether and becomes grim, as if seriousness were the same thing as sanctity. Genesis 21:6 forbids it: God hath made me to laugh. The covenant child's very name is a laugh. And Luke 6 does not abolish laughter but reschedules it — woe to those who laugh now, blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh. The saints are not the people who never laugh. They are the people who laugh last.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsachaq (H6711), to laugh — the root of the name Isaac; la'ag (H3932), to mock, deride; Greek gelao (G1070), to laugh, in the Lord's promised reversal.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsachaq (H6711) — to laugh, whether in unbelief (Gen 18:12) or in joy (Gen 21:6); the root of Yitzchaq, Isaac.
Hebrew la'ag (H3932) — to mock, deride, laugh to scorn; the scorners of Neh 2:19 and Psa 2:4, where the LORD Himself derides.
Greek gelao (G1070) — to laugh; in Luk 6:21 the promise, in Luk 6:25 the woe — the same act, different timing.
usage: “God hath made me to laugh” — the covenant child is named after his mother's joy.
“They laughed us to scorn, and despised us” — the sneer that substitutes for argument.
“Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep” — the reversal is scheduled.

pos: n. (freedom from labour, pain, or disquiet; rendering Hebrew sha'anan, shalev, Greek anapauo)
etymology: From Old French aise, comfort, opportunity. In the Authorized Version the phrase at ease is nearly always a warning label.
biblical_def: Ease is untroubled comfort, and Scripture's judgment on it depends entirely on whether God gave it or a man secured it for himself. There is a promised ease: “His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth” (Psa 25:13). But far more often the phrase marks men ripe for judgment. Amos delivers the classic indictment — “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion” (Amo 6:1) — the deadliest ease being religious ease, comfort inside the covenant community with no fear of God in it. Moab is the object lesson: “Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees” (Jer 48:11), the image of wine left undisturbed until it goes thick and foul. Ease uninterrupted does not preserve a soul; it curdles one. And the rich fool speaks the phrase in its purest form: take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry (Luk 12:19) — on the last night of his life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ease as rest, freedom from labour or pain, tranquillity, and also facility — noting the moral danger of ease that becomes carelessness.
webster_full: EASE, n. Rest; an undisturbed state; applied to the body, freedom from pain, disturbance or annoyance.
2. Applied to the mind, a quiet state; tranquillity; freedom from pain, concern, anxiety, solicitude.
3. Rest from labor.
4. Facility; freedom from difficulty or great labor; easiness.
scriptures: Amo 6:1
Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!

Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth.
corruption_summary: Comfort elevated to the organizing goal of a life and a ministry, so that the woe pronounced on ease in Zion now reads as a description of the average Western congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 6:1 is uncomfortably addressed. The woe does not fall on Babylon but on Zion — on the covenant people, at ease, trusting in the mountain of Samaria, named chief of the nations. That is a religious culture with resources, reputation, and no alarm. A ministry organized around the comfort of its attenders, measuring success by how little is asked, is the thing Amos names. And the therapeutic register supplies the vocabulary to bless it, so that self-protection can be spoken of as wisdom and softness as health.

Jeremiah's image is the sharper diagnosis. Moab was never emptied from vessel to vessel, and so his taste remained in him. Undisturbed ease preserves a man's sin exactly as it was; only the pouring changes the flavour. This reframes affliction: the decanting a believer resents is the very process by which the lees are left behind. Psalm 25:13 shows the ease that is safe — a soul dwelling at ease because it fears the LORD, which is ease received rather than ease secured.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'anan (H7599), to be at ease, careless, secure; shalev (H7961), quiet, tranquil; Greek anapauo (G373), to give rest — the rich fool's word to his soul.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'anan (H7599) — at ease, and often thereby careless; the word carries its own warning (Amo 6:1; Isa 32:9).
Hebrew shalev (H7961) — quiet, at rest; used of Moab settled on his lees (Jer 48:11) and of Job before his affliction.
Greek anapauo (G373) — to cause to rest; the rich fool commands his own soul to rest, a word only Christ may lawfully speak (Mat 11:28).
usage: “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion” — the deadliest comfort is religious comfort.
“Moab hath been at ease from his youth… therefore his taste remained in him” — undisturbed sin keeps its flavour.
“Take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry” — spoken the night his soul was required.

pos: n. (bodily or mental suffering; rendering Hebrew chil, makob, Greek odune, ponos)
etymology: From Latin poena, penalty, punishment, through Old French peine. The etymology preaches: pain entered the world as a penalty, and Scripture never treats it as merely mechanical.
biblical_def: Pain in Scripture is chiefly the pain of travail, and that is a deliberate choice of imagery. Isaiah reaches for it again and again — the nations are “in pain as a woman that travaileth” (Isa 13:8), and Israel's own futility is confessed in the same figure: “we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” (Isa 26:18). The image is exact, because travail is pain with an end in view, pain that is producing something. That is the difference between biblical pain and mere torment. David prays over his honestly: “Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins” (Psa 25:18) — refusing to separate his suffering from his sin, and bringing both to the same throne. Job feels it in the body and mourns in the soul (Job 14:22). And the canon closes by abolishing it: “neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” (Rev 21:4). Pain has a terminus, and a Person appointed to end it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pain first as punishment or penalty — the primary sense — and then as uneasiness or distress of body or mind, noting that labour and travail are its proper biblical figures.
webster_full: PAIN, n. Punishment suffered or denounced; penalty. We say, a law is made on pain of death.
2. Bodily suffering; uneasiness or distress of body of any kind.
3. Uneasiness of mind; disquietude; anxiety; solicitude for the future; grief; sorrow.
4. The throes of childbirth. She bowed herself and travailed, for her pains came upon her.
scriptures: Rev 21:4
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins.
We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.
But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn.
corruption_summary: Pain treated as the one self-evident evil, so that its avoidance becomes the highest good and any doctrine that permits it is judged cruel — the argument beneath euthanasia and beneath the denial of hell alike.
corruption_paragraphs: Make pain the ultimate evil and a whole theology follows. If suffering is the worst thing, then a God who ordains it cannot be good, and the doctrines of providence, of the cross, and of eternal punishment all fall together. The same premise, applied at the bedside, argues that a life in pain may be ended, and applied in the pulpit, argues that hell must be emptied. Scripture's valuation is different and steadier: pain is a real evil, an intruder from the fall, penalty in its root sense — and it is not the worst thing. Sin is.

Isaiah's travail-image supplies the recovery. Pain in the hands of God is productive, not merely destructive; it is going somewhere. Yet Isaiah 26:18 is scrupulously honest that pain apart from God produces nothing at all — all that labour, and the nation brought forth wind. That is the difference between chastening and mere hurt. And the promise of Revelation 21:4 is not that the saints will learn to reinterpret their pain, but that God will wipe it away entirely, having Himself borne the penalty the word means.
roots_summary: Hebrew chil (H2342), to writhe or travail; makob (H4341), pain, sorrow — the word of Isaiah 53, acquainted with grief; Greek ponos (G4192), toilsome pain, abolished in Rev 21:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew chil (H2342) — to twist, writhe, travail; the standing prophetic image for national anguish (Isa 13:8; Isa 26:17).
Hebrew makob (H4341) — pain, sorrow; the plural stands in Isa 53:3, the Man of sorrows acquainted with grief.
Greek ponos (G4192) — toil, anguish, pain; named among the former things passed away (Rev 21:4).
usage: “Neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” — pain has a terminus.
“Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins” — David brings both to one throne.
“We have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” — travail apart from God produces nothing.
